issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking inheritance must prove when the person whose estate is claimed died if that fact is essential to the succession, because the presumption arising from prolonged absence does not establish the exact time of death.
material_facts: The claimant sought succession to a person's estate as a collateral relative.
The person had not been heard from for more than seven years.
The claimant neither pleaded nor proved the date of that person's death.
issues.conclusion: The claimant did not establish that succession to the estate had opened by the date the suit was filed, and the lower courts erred in treating the suit filing date as the date of death.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 107 and 108 of the Evidence Act, prolonged absence may give rise to a presumption of death, but Section 108 does not presume the exact time of death. The person claiming a right for which the date of death is essential bears the burden of proving that date. The Court relied on Sri Vidya Mandir Education Society (Regd.) v. Malleswaram Sangeetha Sabha and Others, which noticed Lal Chand Marwari v. Mahant Ramrup Gir and Another.

predicates.succession_claim: A person sought to inherit an estate through a claimed relationship to the person whose estate was at issue.
predicates.death_date_essential_to_claim: The claimed succession depended on establishing when the person whose estate was claimed died.
predicates.exact_death_date_not_proved: The claimant did not establish the exact date of that person's death.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks succession and the date of death is essential but unproved, the claimant's succession is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer's exclusive possession of jointly held property does not become adverse to the other co-sharers without a clear ouster, and mutation alone does not establish ouster unless it clearly denies their title.
material_facts: A successor to one co-sharer and, later, that successor's descendants possessed the land, including the share claimed by other collaterals, from 1930.
The descendants obtained mutation of their names after the claims of the claimant and other collaterals had been rejected.
The predecessor mortgaged part of the land and sold part of it while treating himself as owner.
The appellants' possession was continuous for more than the statutory period, public, and adverse to the other collaterals.
issues.conclusion: The appellants established clear ouster and adverse possession, perfected title to the disputed land, and the appeal was allowed with the trial court's dismissal of the suit restored.
issues.legal_principle: Possession by one co-sharer is ordinarily treated as possession on behalf of all co-sharers. Adverse possession against the others requires a clear ouster through denial of their title; mutation in one co-sharer's name is insufficient unless accompanied by a clear declaration denying the others' title. The Court discussed Sardar Amar Singh v. Sardarni Shiv Datt Kaur and Bashir Ahmad & Ors. v. Parshottam & Ors., and stated the ouster rule as the correct legal position.

rule.if: co_sharer_adverse_possession_claim and exclusive_possession_by_one_co_sharer and clear_ouster_of_other_co_sharers and open_hostile_possession and statutory_period_elapsed

predicates.co_sharer_adverse_possession_claim: A party in a dispute over co-shared property claimed to have acquired title by adverse possession against the other co-sharers.
predicates.exclusive_possession_by_one_co_sharer: One co-sharer or that co-sharer's successors possessed the whole or disputed part of the property.
predicates.clear_ouster_of_other_co_sharers: The possessor clearly denied the other co-sharers' title, including through a declaration or conduct that made the denial clear.
predicates.open_hostile_possession: The possessor's possession was public and adverse to the other co-sharers rather than held on their behalf.
predicates.statutory_period_elapsed: The adverse possession continued for the legally required period.

issues.definition: When a co-sharer claiming adverse possession exclusively possesses property, clearly ousts the other co-sharers, and openly maintains hostile possession for the required period, title is perfected by adverse possession.
